claims.text: Retention of high toughness in high-entropy alloys is governed by the formation of nanoscale chemical short-range-order clusters.
Nanoscale SRO clusters retard localized dislocation pile-up.
Nanoscale SRO clusters retard crack initiation.
SRO clusters act as distributed barriers to strain localization and thereby promote more homogeneous plastic flow.
Rapid solidification or quenching of single-phase equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi can produce a largely chemically disordered microstructure with minimal SRO.
An intermediate-temperature annealing treatment can enhance SRO without causing secondary-phase precipitation.
A higher-temperature or excessively long annealing treatment dissolves SRO.
The spatial distribution of nanoscale SRO clusters regulates dislocation motion.
SRO clusters raise local yield strength by retarding dislocation pile-up.
The strengthening associated with SRO leads to distributed plastic deformation and crack deflection.
Disrupting SRO clusters through overannealing removes their barrier effect.
Loss of the SRO barrier effect causes more localized deformation, earlier crack propagation, and lower toughness.
Thermal treatments that produce moderate SRO will increase fracture toughness relative to the as-quenched baseline.
Treatments that suppress or dissolve SRO will reduce toughness.
The as-quenched alloy has a predominantly random chemical distribution, limited preexisting SRO, and moderate toughness.
The proposed mechanism applies to single-phase equiatomic high-entropy alloys such as CoCrFeMnNi when secondary-phase precipitation and excessive grain-boundary segregation are avoided.
The mechanism applies within sub-melting-point annealing windows where SRO evolution is kinetically favored.
